title: Team Members Who Only See the Small Picture
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post addresses team members who fixate on immediate details and never connect their work to the larger strategy. The author says this narrowness limits their path into leadership, and that good leaders deliberately widen it rather than settle for worker bees. Three tools are offered: include them in strategic discussions, ask them to map their tasks to long-range goals visually, and have them benchmark against other organizations. The mapping exercise also surfaces unintended consequences of everyday choices. The closing argument is that success depends on connections, and that nobody will trust a person to lead who cannot envision the future.
points: Narrow focus on short-term tasks blocks a team member's growth into leadership, so widening perspective is a leader's responsibility.
Repeated exposure to strategy conversations gradually draws quiet, myopic people into contributing and connecting the dots.
Having someone draw how their work links to long-range goals, and leaving the visual in place, makes the connection concrete and reveals unintended consequences.
Benchmarking against competitors broadens a person's view of what best practice looks like and how their work compares.
quotes: They focus on the small details, the short-term, the issues that are directly at hand, and the actions that must be taken immediately. They don’t look up and connect the dots. The bigger picture eludes them.

They need everyone to understand the implications of their work on the desired outcomes of the enterprise. By broadening the perspective of a myopic team member to see the bigger picture, leaders prepare them to make a larger contribution in the future.

Doing this on paper or a whiteboard and leaving the visual behind reinforces the need to understand the implications of their work. This exercise also lends itself to exploring the possible unintended consequences of their everyday choices, further expanding their view.

This encourages them to assess the impact of their work compared to those at competing organizations. Learning about a competitor’s everyday practices and what makes them “best practices” also leads to a broader view.
A team member’s success is all about connections. Everything they do to connect to other people, to the work at hand, and to the big picture enhances their ability to succeed.
Keeping the big picture in mind opens the eyes to what is possible. We don’t trust anyone to lead who can’t envision the future.
